body.text: Just a few months ago the grand old man of Australian political journalism, Paul Kelly, published the final instalment of a self-described trilogy of books about federal governments of the past three decades. Beginning with an account of the epic rivalry between Paul Keating and John Howard (The March of Patriots: The Struggle for Modern Australia) it was followed by a narrative of how things went awry during the Kevin Rudd/Julia Gillard era (Triumph and Demise: The Broken Promise of a Labor Generation). The recently published third volume, the gloomiest of them all, focuses on the Tony Abbott/Malcolm Turnbull/Scott Morrison prime ministerships (The Twilight of Exceptionalism: The Liberal and Conservative Era).

As its title suggests, that concluding book is a story of political fall, a tale drastically short of the heroic reformers — Bob Hawke, Paul Keating and John Howard — who came before them. Kelly’s fundamental thesis is that a period in which that trio of prime-ministerial titans led Australia on a path of “exceptionalism” gave way to a series of successors who squandered their legacy and condemned the nation to decline.

So pessimistic is Kelly that he sombrely pronounced at last month’s Canberra Writers Festival — on a panel of which I was part — that the country needed a “circuit breaker.” This, he suggested, could come in one or more of three ways: the rousing effects of artificial intelligence, a war, or an economic depression. I couldn’t help but think the nation was being invited to choose its own poison.

There is no gainsaying Kelly’s elevated place in Australian political journalism and history writing over the past half century. Starting with his grippingly forensic 1976 account of the demise of Gough Whitlam’s Labor government (The Unmaking of Gough), his output has been not only staggering in its scale but profoundly influential. As Frank Bongiorno rightly observed in his Inside Story review, The Twilight of Exceptionalism “and the larger body of work of which it forms a part, is an exceptional contribution to the history of modern Australian politics.”

While I don’t wish to devalue Kelly’s mighty legacy, I believe his notion of a modern “Australian exceptionalism” should be contested. Associated with his best-known book, The End of Certainty: Power, Politics & Business in Australia (1992), the concept is mainly celebratory of the economic reform era of Labor’s Hawke and Keating. What did this “Australian exceptionalism” comprise? In a nutshell, it was the market economic reforms — with a distinctive national spin — ushered in under Hawke, Keating and later Howard. If there is any question about this, he puts it beyond doubt in the introduction of his latest book: “This was the age of Australian Exceptionalism, when the nation was reshaped by bold governments and astute leaders, the upshot being productivity gains, while alert to equity needs.”

Further on in that introduction, Kelly approvingly quotes a similarly down-in-the-mouth Howard government treasurer, Peter Costello, to reinforce the point that he conceives Australian exceptionalism as synonymous with market-focused economic reform and management:

Australian Exceptionalism became a phrase used in the IMF [International Monetary Fund]. We were considered a model by other Western nations. The process began with Hawke and Keating but the fiscal high point — ten budget surpluses and the retirement of all commonwealth debt — was considered to be Australian Exceptionalism. What we have lost is the idea that Australia can be exceptional. The idea that Australia can lead the world has disappeared. I feel it is the end of an era, when Australia was exceptional but does not see itself as exceptional anymore.
Boiled down, then, Australian exceptionalism at its apotheosis was budget surpluses and debt retirement.

One immediate problem with such a claim is that the final years of the Howard government were a period of fiscal profligacy. As George Megalogenis highlights in his recent book, Three Shocks, Australia at the beginning of the 2000s was, to put it colloquially, bitten on the bum by a rainbow. China’s surging economic development flooded the nation’s coffers with revenue from iron ore, coal and other exports. Rather than bank much of that bonanza, the Howard government splurged it on spending and tax concessions that favoured the privileged in areas like education, housing and superannuation — the spending Howard’s successors have had so much trouble clawing back.

A more significant problem with Kelly/Costello exceptionalism, however, is that it shrinks it essentially to economic stewardship. More than that, its correlation with market reforms strains against longer-run understandings of what has been distinctive about the country’s political economy and politics.

Here, I should insert a caveat. The very concept of a national exceptionalism is almost invariably shot through with contradictions and permeated by wishful thinking, if not mythology. For instance, the Anzac Legend that Australians have genuflected to for more than a century revolves around the idea that our soldiers exhibited traits born of, and peculiar to, this society, namely, mateship, resourcefulness and an egalitarian-fuelled disrespect for authority. Yet, as historians have long recognised, these characteristics are not unique to the martial folklore of this land: other cultures ascribe similar qualities to their warriors.

Nevertheless, Australia’s political economy and politics have distinguishing features. The late historian John Hirst wrote persuasively about the distinctive and contradictory elements of Australia’s democratic culture. On the one hand, this is a country that has been heavily reliant on and trusting in the benevolence of government — a country whose people readily comply with laws and rules. (Australia was, for instance, the first nation to make seatbelt-wearing compulsory.) Yet politicians are the object of popular scorn and Australians imagine themselves as anti-authoritarian. Hirst coined the phrase a “democracy of manners” to describe a country that was not so much egalitarian in its distribution of income and wealth as characterised by a lack of formality and airs in how different stratas of society related to one another.

I want to pick up another thread of Australian exceptionalism. When I was a callow undergraduate at Monash University, I was introduced to the Hartz “fragment” thesis. In simple terms, the American political scientist Louis Hartz proposed that the timing of a settler society’s founding largely determined its political culture. As “fragments” were flung off from Europe and freed from ideological competition, the foundation ideas congealed in the settler societies and reigned supreme.

The United States, for instance, was born in an age when John Locke’s reification of individual rights was flourishing, and that spirit was universalised in American society and became virtually impregnable. Australia’s early white settlement, on the other hand, coincided with the blooming of the ideas of Jeremy Bentham and utilitarianism philosophy, with its cornerstone tenet of the greatest happiness for the greatest number. Coalescing with that mood was the ferment of the nineteenth-century radical-democratic Chartist movement.

The result in Australia, it was suggested, was a collectivist majoritarian Zeitgeist and an expansive view of the responsibilities and role of government. According to the Hartz thesis, the relatively easy triumph of a utilitarian culture in Australia meant that radical thought atrophied: it emerged devoid of a doctrinaire edge. Australia became a pragmatic, egalitarian-minded society predisposed to government involvement yet inhospitable to theory and theorists.

Like any epic schema, Hartz’s thesis has imperfections. But it also has a beguiling kernel of truth. Majoritarian-orientated and practical-minded, Australia has been a country averse to ideological extremes or demagogues, a nation open to curtailing individual rights and intervening in the marketplace in the name of the common good. As Judith Brett shows in her wonderful history of Australia’s electoral system, a pronounced colonial-era reliance on government for economic development reinforced the majoritarian ethic, which went hand in hand with a bureaucratic political culture. The accompanying propensity for electoral experimentation began with the pioneering innovation of the secret ballot (known overseas as the Australian ballot) and culminated with the adoption of compulsory voting in 1924.

The latter would be inconceivable in the ferociously individualistic United States, with its terror of a tyranny of the majority. Nor is compulsory voting present in the other anglophone countries to which Australia is typically compared: Britain, Canada and New Zealand. That the practice not only was implemented in this country but also has been settled policy for a century can be read as confirmation of a distinctiveness to the political culture that doesn’t hold individual liberties to be sacrosanct.

A case can also be made that the belief in an enabling state and a levelling social compact crystallised with the birth of the new nation at the beginning of the twentieth century. We shouldn’t be triumphalist about that settlement: its focus was on protecting the living standards of white male breadwinners, with First Nations peoples brutally and shamefully marginalised. Despite its original sins, though, there was much that was novel and progressive about the nation-building edifice laid down at that time.

Alfred Deakin, three-time prime minister in the first decade of the Commonwealth, was chief architect — mostly in alliance with the fledgling Labor Party — of policies and institutions aimed at evening out the life chances of citizens. As a Victorian, he borrowed heavily from that colony’s experiments in independent wage-setting, industrial arbitration, workplace protections and rudimentary welfare in the latter nineteenth century. That Melbourne was the capital of the new nation during its first quarter century helped facilitate the Victorian supremacy over politics and policy. As Marilyn Lake and other historians have shown, the innovative, socially liberal measures enacted in Australia during that time inspired fascination internationally. The young antipodean societies were viewed from abroad as a thrilling alternative to the musty class inequalities and entrenched privileges of the Old World.

Let’s not exaggerate this picture. The optimism of that glad confident morning, the first decade of the Commonwealth, was snuffed out for a lengthy period by cataclysmic war and depression. Indeed, it was only when the postwar reconstruction program — what historian Stuart Macintyre termed “Australia’s Boldest Experiment” — was launched in the 1940s under Labor’s John Curtin and Ben Chifley that the country’s majoritarian project was reinvigorated by Keynesian economic management, with its centrepiece of full employment and an enhanced welfare state.

During the extended reign of Curtin and Chifley’s prime-ministerial successor, the Liberal behemoth Robert Menzies — so long miscast by his Labor opponents as a public policy plodder — the postwar government-managed economy was preserved in partnership with private enterprise. Under this balanced dispensation, Australia joined much of the Western industrial world in a period of expanding prosperity and constrained inequality.

Later, following the glorious effusion of the Whitlam era when Indigenous Australians and other groups hitherto excluded from the nation’s social compact were invited in, Keynesian economics hit its limits and the postwar settlement unravelled. Following an interregnum of Gramscian-like “morbid symptoms,” with governments not quite knowing how to respond to the scourge of stagflation, neoliberalism slipped in to fill its place.

This was the era of ascendant market economics, and it was Kelly, of course, who became its chief amanuensis with his sprawling and undeniably brilliant account, The End of Certainty. By his reckoning — a view mostly in lockstep with that of Keating, the spellbinding salesperson of the Labor government’s economic reforms of the 1980s — this was a decade of breaking from the dead hand of history. Only by overthrowing the sclerotic policies and institutions instigated at the outset of the Commonwealth (the so-called “Australian Settlement”), the argument went, could the country reap its full economic and social potential. It was a seductive story, even if the idea of an “Australian Settlement” was always something of a straw man.

The major reforms of that period of economic internationalisation and deregulation were mostly necessary as well as inevitable. Because it was a Labor government in the vanguard of those changes, with Hawke and Keating supported by a highly talented cabinet, that far-reaching renovation of the economy and society also had a distinctively Australian twist. The government’s laudable objective was to harmonise the unleashing of productive market forces with safeguards including Medicare, carefully targeted welfare measures and compulsory superannuation. To that extent, it was a kind of meeting between neoliberalism and Australian exceptionalism.

Yet the unshielding of Australia from the global economy and the supercharging of market forces did strain the country’s majoritarian culture and stress-test its egalitarian social compact. Despite worthy reforms such as the introduction of the GST, the Howard government’s free-market push was conducted with less attention to equality. The privatisation agenda was accelerated, workplace protections were weakened and market provision was encouraged in school education, childcare, aged care and health insurance that over time licenced corporate excesses, favoured the privileged and seeded widening inequality. It is also the case that much of the neoliberal agenda was pursued in the face of lingering misgivings by a public inclined to see them as having been foisted on them by unfeeling ivory tower–style elites. The rash of privatisations were especially resented.

Of course, there is no simple cause and effect between the sweeping economic reforms of the late twentieth century and the strains now abundant in Australian society. In the opening of his new book, Kelly presents a compelling synthesis of what currently ails the country and why “governing in the national interest had become much more difficult.” His survey ranges over factors including the coarsening and polarising of public discourse caused by the emergence of social media, the rise of performative politics, the global instability triggered by the challenge of China and the declining reliability and prestige of Washington, the hollowing out of the major parties, a decline in quality of the public service and the ubiquity of social identity politics (of which he is no fan).

Into that potent mix Kelly adds the demise of “the Christian compact,” which has undermined shared values and occurred in tandem with a waning of respect for traditional authority generally. With a potent elegiac note he writes lugubriously about “a new and powerful centrifugalism — the erosion of the centre, the flight away from nearly every organised centre of authority, control and virtue.” He goes on: “There was a new, often narcissistic individualism, reinforced by the rise of personal autonomy and the cult that ‘being true to myself’ was the ultimate moral stance.”

Though the challenges Kelly identifies are real, the apocalyptic picture he paints has more than a whiff of an elderly man estranged from, and struggling to understand, the society evolving around him. It’s true that younger generations are less inclined to hold to traditional religious faiths, for example, but this doesn’t mean they have no strong belief systems and convictions. One of the defining features of Millennials and Gen Zers is their robust tolerance of others and respect for diversity.

While impressive in its breadth, Kelly’s account of the forces bedevilling contemporary Australia also has some striking omissions. Perhaps for understandable reasons, he is silent on the role of the dominant player in the country’s media landscape, Rupert Murdoch’s News Corp. Since early this century, News Corp has retreated from the principle of balanced coverage to embark on the equivalent of a search-and-destroy mission against left-of-centre politics and other sections of the media that have the temerity not to share its ideological view. The unbridled partisanship and vendettas waged by the Murdoch outlets have stimulated a growing chasm between progressive and conservative media and an associated diminution of meaningful community-wide political debate and genuine exchange of ideas.

Most conspicuously missing from Kelly’s account, however, are the effects of the market-reform period itself. Here, I suspect, he is hoist on his own analytical petard. Having so vociferously cheered on these reforms and, indeed, holding to the view that the solution to Australia’s present economic travails is further changes in that direction, Kelly can’t bring himself to entertain the idea that they have had some deleterious consequences. He obdurately declines to acknowledge that a byproduct of those market-oriented reforms was the atomisation of society and rampant individualism he so abhors.

Yet Australians are daily presented with evidence of the shameless unapologetic avarice of the corporate oligopolies that dominate markets, the failures of private providers of childcare and other services, a school-funding system that means some of our children are educated in obscene splendour and others in public squalor, and the pauperisation of sections of the workforce, including those delivering essential services in the care economy. Inequality will always be with us, but we are in a time when the disparities of opportunity along class, generation and geographical lines are not only glaringly obvious to Australians but offensive to the nation’s traditional, albeit flawed and incomplete, attachment to a “fair go.”

This is where I most diverge from Kelly. For him, recapturing Australia’s “exceptionalism” means swallowing the medicine of further market-driven economic reform. The changes of the late twentieth century were certainly bold and brave, even if largely unavoidable, but they were also contingent, contested and messy, and never simply a story of heroic leaders gripped by penetrating visions bestriding the land. Nor can that set of prime ministers be held chiefly responsible for problems that now afflict the country. While they released forces that grew problematic over time, it is their successors, too often asleep at the wheel, who allowed them to fester.

My fundamental point is that Australian exceptionalism can and should be read more broadly. A longer-term tradition of majoritarianism has been expressed most influentially, I’d argue, in an enabling state committed to evening out the life chances of citizens. This is the tradition that needs new life breathed into it.

It won’t be easy. Paul Kelly is indisputably right when he contends that governing productively and forging a consensus for reform is significantly more difficult in the twenty-first century. Moreover, we are at a point when, in an echo of the 1970s, no clear model exists to meet pressing challenges. It will require imagination and innovation: much as it did more than a century ago when this land was seen as a progressive beacon. And that creativity mustn’t only be confined to ideas and actions. Persuasive advocacy is also desperately needed.

Somewhere along the way prime ministers in this country appear to have lost sight of the fact that effective rhetoric is a lifeblood of political leadership. Anthony Albanese and his colleagues need to move beyond their habitual anodyne oratorical practices to speak truth to the public about power and privilege. A good starting point would be to recalibrate the national conversation away from endless numbing recitations of a “cost-of-living crisis” and talk about inequality. Because — and I reckon most members of the public recognise this in their heart of hearts — that is the malady Australia truly confronts. •
